title: Transaction Structuring (Smurfing)
description: Structuring involves deliberately breaking a large financial transaction into smaller amounts, typically below regulatory reporting thresholds such as the $10,000 CTR threshold under the Bank Secrecy Act. The goal is to avoid triggering automatic reports to FinCEN. Indicators include multiple transactions in rapid succession from the same account, round or just-below-threshold amounts, and consistent patterns over several days. Structuring is illegal under 31 U.S.C. § 5324 regardless of whether the underlying funds are lawful.
indicators: Multiple transactions just below $10,000
Round amounts (e.g., $9,000, $9,500)
Same sender account within 24-48 hours
High transaction velocity with consistent amounts
Cash deposits split across multiple branches
regulatoryReference: 31 U.S.C. § 5324; BSA/AML CTR threshold ($10,000); FinCEN Advisory FIN-2014-A007
exampleScenario: An account holder makes five separate $9,500 cash deposits across three branches within two days, totaling $47,500. Each transaction individually falls below the $10,000 CTR threshold, but the pattern clearly indicates an intent to evade reporting requirements.

title: Money Mule Account Activity
description: A money mule is an individual who transfers illegally obtained funds on behalf of others, often unknowingly recruited through fake job offers or romance scams. The mule's account receives large inflows from multiple sources and rapidly distributes funds to other accounts, often internationally. Key indicators include a sudden increase in transaction volume, funds received from unknown sources followed by near-immediate outgoing transfers, and a high ratio of incoming to outgoing transactions with minimal account balance retention.
indicators: Sudden spike in account activity
Large inflows from multiple unrelated sources
Near-immediate redistribution of received funds
Minimal balance retention between transfers
New account with high-value activity
International wire transfers shortly after domestic deposits
regulatoryReference: FATF Typology Report on Money Laundering; EU 6th Anti-Money Laundering Directive (6AMLD); FinCEN SAR Filing Guidance
exampleScenario: A recently opened account receives three wire transfers totaling $150,000 from different corporate accounts within one week. Within hours of each receipt, the account holder initiates international wire transfers to accounts in high-risk jurisdictions, retaining less than 2% of the transferred amount.

title: Account Takeover (ATO) Fraud
description: Account takeover occurs when a fraudster gains unauthorized access to a legitimate customer's account, typically through phishing, credential stuffing, or social engineering. The attacker then initiates unauthorized transactions, changes account settings, or extracts funds. Key indicators include transactions from unusual geographic locations, changes to contact information followed by high-value transfers, transactions at unusual times for the account holder, and sudden deviations from established spending patterns.
indicators: Transactions from new geographic location or device
Contact information changes followed by large transfers
Transactions at unusual hours for the account holder
Password reset followed by immediate high-value transfer
Spending patterns drastically different from historical baseline
Multiple failed login attempts preceding successful access
regulatoryReference: Regulation E (12 CFR § 1005); FFIEC Guidance on Authentication; PSD2 Strong Customer Authentication (EU)
exampleScenario: A customer's account, which typically processes domestic payments of $200-$500, suddenly initiates a $45,000 wire transfer to an overseas account at 3:00 AM local time. The account email was changed 30 minutes before the transfer, and there were 12 failed login attempts from a foreign IP address in the preceding hour.

title: Layering (Money Laundering Stage 2)
description: Layering is the second stage of money laundering, designed to distance illicit funds from their criminal source through complex layers of financial transactions. The goal is to obscure the audit trail. Techniques include rapid movement of funds between multiple accounts (often across jurisdictions), conversion between different financial instruments, use of shell companies, and round-tripping through trade-based transactions. The complexity and speed of transactions are the primary hallmarks.
indicators: Rapid fund movement through multiple accounts
Cross-border transfers to/from high-risk jurisdictions
Circular transactions (funds returning to origin through intermediaries)
Use of multiple shell company accounts
Frequent currency conversions
Transactions with no clear economic purpose
regulatoryReference: FATF 40 Recommendations; 4th EU Anti-Money Laundering Directive; BSA/AML Examination Manual
exampleScenario: Funds totaling $500,000 move through seven different accounts across four countries within 48 hours. The money passes through two shell companies registered in offshore jurisdictions, undergoes two currency conversions, and ultimately arrives in an investment account bearing no obvious connection to the original sender.

title: Bust-Out Fraud (Credit/Account Fraud)
description: Bust-out fraud involves building up trust and credit over time before maximizing credit lines and absconding with the funds. In the context of transaction monitoring, bust-out patterns manifest as accounts that maintain normal, low-risk activity for months, gradually increase transaction sizes and frequency, then suddenly execute a burst of high-value transactions before the account goes dormant or is abandoned. This pattern exploits the trust signals that normal account history creates.
indicators: Gradual increase in transaction amounts over weeks/months
Sudden spike to maximum transaction capacity
Account goes dormant immediately after high-value burst
Balance drawn to zero or negative
Historical activity used to establish credibility
Multiple payment methods utilized during bust-out phase
regulatoryReference: OCC Bulletin 2019-37; FinCEN Mortgage Fraud SAR Activity Review
exampleScenario: An account shows 8 months of regular $500-$2,000 monthly transfers. Over two weeks, transaction amounts escalate to $15,000, then $40,000. In a 72-hour window, the account initiates $280,000 in outgoing transfers, depleting all available funds. The account holder becomes unreachable and the account is abandoned.

title: Trade-Based Money Laundering (TBML)
description: Trade-based money laundering exploits international trade transactions to move value across borders. Methods include over-invoicing or under-invoicing goods, multiple invoicing for the same shipment, and phantom shipments where no goods actually move. In transaction monitoring, TBML manifests as payments that don't match typical trade patterns: amounts inconsistent with the type or volume of goods, payments to/from counterparties in high-risk jurisdictions with no clear business relationship, and discrepancies between declared trade values and market prices.
indicators: Payment amounts inconsistent with goods/services described
Transactions with counterparties in known TBML jurisdictions
Repeated payments for same invoice or shipment
Significant over/under-pricing compared to market rates
Payments routed through intermediary countries
No corresponding trade documentation
regulatoryReference: FATF Report on Trade-Based Money Laundering (2006); FinCEN Advisory FIN-2010-A001; Wolfsberg Group Trade Finance Principles
exampleScenario: A company makes monthly payments of $200,000 to a supplier in a high-risk jurisdiction for 'electronic components.' Market analysis shows the declared unit prices are 400% above market rates. The receiving company has no web presence and was incorporated 3 months before the first transaction.

title: Rapid Fund Movement (Pass-Through Activity)
description: Rapid fund movement describes accounts that function primarily as pass-through conduits, receiving and disbursing funds within a very short timeframe. Unlike money mule activity, this pattern may involve legitimate business accounts being misused, or accounts specifically created for fund transit. The hallmark is the minimal dwell time of funds in the account — typically less than 24 hours between receipt and disbursement — with the account maintaining a near-zero balance between transaction cycles.
indicators: Funds disbursed within hours of receipt
Near-zero balance between transaction cycles
High transaction volume relative to account age
Incoming and outgoing amounts nearly identical (minus small fees)
Regular pattern of receive-then-send behavior
No legitimate business explanation for pass-through activity
regulatoryReference: FinCEN SAR Narrative Guidance; FATF Risk-Based Approach Guidance; BSA/AML Examination Manual Section on Suspicious Activity
exampleScenario: An account receives a $75,000 wire transfer at 9:15 AM and initiates three outgoing transfers totaling $74,500 by 11:30 AM the same day. This pattern repeats 4 times within 10 days, with funds never remaining in the account for more than 3 hours.

title: Cash-Intensive Business Anomalies
description: Cash-intensive businesses (restaurants, retail, car washes, parking garages) can be exploited to commingle illicit cash with legitimate revenue. Suspicious patterns include cash deposits that significantly exceed expected revenue for the business type and size, deposits that remain constant regardless of seasonal variations, and cash deposit patterns that don't match business operating hours or customer traffic patterns. The key is the deviation between expected and actual cash flows.
indicators: Cash deposits exceeding industry norms for business size
Consistent deposit amounts regardless of seasonal trends
Cash deposits at times inconsistent with business hours
Revenue reported significantly higher than peer businesses
No corresponding increase in business expenses with increased revenue
Round deposit amounts suggesting manual calculation rather than actual cash receipts
regulatoryReference: FinCEN Geographic Targeting Orders; BSA/AML Examination Manual; IRS Cash-Intensive Business Audit Techniques Guide
exampleScenario: A small restaurant with 30 seats reports weekly cash deposits of $45,000 — three times the industry average for a restaurant its size. Deposits occur every Monday and Thursday at exactly the same amount, regardless of holidays or seasonal variations, and the business reports no corresponding increase in supply purchases.

title: Insider Threat / Employee Fraud
description: Insider fraud occurs when employees or authorized personnel abuse their access to financial systems for personal gain or to facilitate criminal activity. In transaction monitoring, insider threats manifest as transactions initiated outside normal business processes, unauthorized account modifications, transactions that bypass normal approval chains, and patterns suggesting an employee is testing system controls before executing larger fraudulent transactions. Insider fraud often exploits gaps in segregation of duties.
indicators: Transactions initiated outside normal business hours by employees
Account modifications not following standard procedures
Small test transactions preceding larger unauthorized transfers
Employee accounts with unusual transaction patterns
Transactions bypassing normal approval workflows
Access to accounts outside employee's normal responsibilities
regulatoryReference: FFIEC IT Examination Handbook; Sarbanes-Oxley Act Section 302/404; COSO Internal Control Framework
exampleScenario: A bank employee modifies the daily transfer limit on a dormant corporate account at 11:45 PM, then initiates a $200,000 transfer to a personal account at 11:58 PM. Three days earlier, the same employee made two $50 test transfers from the same corporate account to verify the transfer mechanism.

title: Unusual Geographic Transaction Patterns
description: Geographic anomalies in transaction patterns can indicate fraud, money laundering, or sanctions evasion. Suspicious geographic patterns include transactions involving countries under sanctions or with weak AML controls, sudden geographic shifts in transaction destinations, transactions that transit through multiple jurisdictions without clear business justification, and activity patterns inconsistent with the customer's known geographic footprint. The risk assessment should consider both the jurisdictions involved and the pattern of geographic movement.
indicators: Transactions to/from FATF high-risk jurisdictions
Sudden change in transaction geography
Funds routed through multiple countries (jurisdiction hopping)
Transactions inconsistent with customer's declared business geography
Wire transfers to newly added foreign beneficiaries
IP address/device location inconsistent with transaction origin
regulatoryReference: OFAC Sanctions Programs; FATF High-Risk Jurisdictions List; EU High-Risk Third Country List; FinCEN Section 311 Special Measures
exampleScenario: A domestic retail business account that has never processed international transactions suddenly initiates wire transfers to accounts in three different high-risk jurisdictions within one week, totaling $180,000. The declared purpose is 'consulting fees,' but the business has no known international operations.
